_note: Editorial layer. Numbers never live here. Match keys are 'Home Manager v Away Manager' exactly as they appear in the derived data.
standfirst: Five fixtures, ten compulsory releases, and a table separated entirely by points scored.

Roscoe Hill v Brad Hill.thirty: Two Hills, three points, and a family Christmas now hanging by a thread. Palmer's 13 was the biggest individual return in the league and it still was not enough, because Brad turned up with four players who all did something.
Roscoe Hill v Brad Hill.verdict: The highest combined total of the week and the narrowest margin of the week, with a surname clash on top. Nothing else on the card came close.
assessment: Brad's 47 was the broadest score in the division. Ødegaard 11, Guéhi 10, Calafiori 9 and Pickford 7 produced 37 between them, more than four other managers managed with a full eleven. Only Ballard blanked.

Roscoe's 44 was built on two men and a hope. Palmer 13 and Barry 8 gave him 21, Raya and Branthwaite another 12, and the remaining seven starters contributed 11. An excellent total assembled alarmingly.

Both benches carried something. Brad had Trafford on 9 behind Pickford on 7, a net loss of two in a fixture he won by three. Roscoe had Kelleher on 7, so his bench was never the problem. His midfield was.
The release rule then takes a bite out of each. Roscoe loses the fixture and the best player in the division on the same afternoon.
Roscoe Hill v Brad Hill.overall: Brad walks away with three points, the top score of the week and a release bill of 11. Roscoe posted the second-highest total in the league, beat nobody, and hands Palmer to the waivers as a parting gift.

Matthew Lees v Piers Rennie.thirty: Matthew benched De Cuyper, who returned 17, and then lost by four. Piers won with a side whose leading scorer managed six, which is less a victory than a clerical error that happened to fall his way.
Matthew Lees v Piers Rennie.verdict: The cruellest result of the week by a distance. One team-sheet decision turned a comfortable win into a defeat, and the beneficiary did almost nothing to deserve it.
assessment: Piers assembled the flattest 35 available to modern science. Gonzalo 6 led the way and no player reached seven. Six of his eleven returned two or fewer. This was not a performance, it was attendance.
Matthew's 31 was carried by Szoboszlai 8, Mosquera 6 and Tzolis 6, which is 20 from three. Eight players for 11 points.

The bench is the whole story. De Cuyper scored 17, more than half of what Matthew's entire eleven produced, and would have won the fixture on his own with room to spare. Nineteen points sat unused in a four-point defeat.
Then the rule twists the knife the wrong way round. Because the release applies to the active eleven only, a 17-point defender stays on his books untouched.
Matthew Lees v Piers Rennie.overall: Piers collects three points and the softest release fee in the division for a score that would have lost to six of the other nine managers.

Michael Lavarack v Matthew Xenakis.thirty: Michael's team is called Average and it scored 37 with Haaland on two, which is either irony or a confession. Gakpo's 12 was the best return on the pitch and Matthew still lost.
Michael Lavarack v Matthew Xenakis.verdict: Three points between two managers who were both rescued by a midfielder and both abandoned by their forwards. Close, competent, quietly humiliating.
assessment: Michael's 37 came from a genuinely wide base. Dewsbury-Hall 11 led it, and a defensive block of Lacroix, Tarkowski and Collins added 18. The attack was the problem and it was not subtle: six players, six points.
Matthew's 34 was violently top-heavy. Gakpo 12 and Rogers 8 gave him 20 and the other nine starters managed 14.
Neither bench had anything to say. Michael's four substitutes scored nothing whatsoever between them, a clean sweep of noughts.
The release rule is where Michael quietly wins twice: he hands back an eleven-point return nobody expects to repeat while the defensive core that actually built his score stays intact.
Michael Lavarack v Matthew Xenakis.overall: Michael leaves with three points and the more replaceable player gone, the only outcome all week that looks deliberate.

Mark Stone v Mattato Alcock.thirty: Mark won by five while leaving Elanga and Vuskovic on the bench with 15 points between them, and his forward line of Isak and Richarlison contributed two each. Mattato's response was to field Gyökeres, who scored nothing.
Mark Stone v Mattato Alcock.verdict: Won and lost by roughly equal quantities of mismanagement. The five-point margin is generous to the standard of decision-making on display.
assessment: Mark's 39 rested on two defenders. White 11 and Gvardiol 9 gave him 20, half his total. The front of the team was effectively absent: Isak, Richarlison and Wirtz for six points between them.
Mattato's 34 followed the same unhappy shape. Ndiaye 9 and King 7 gave him 16, and six other starters produced 14 between them.
Mattato had Verbruggen on 6, a goalkeeper who outscored eight of his own starters, which is a diagnosis rather than a statistic.
Under the release rule Mark gives up White but keeps the two men who actually performed, so his squad barely registers the loss.
Mark Stone v Mattato Alcock.overall: Mark won a fixture he set up badly and emerges with his two best performers still on the books. Mattato loses the match and his top scorer and has no hidden depth to draw on.

Stefano Babiolakis v Nicolas Rubin.thirty: Stefano fielded Watkins, Marmoush and Nicolas Jackson: three forwards, zero points, which takes a level of commitment most people cannot sustain.
Stefano Babiolakis v Nicolas Rubin.verdict: The lowest score of the week against a comfortable winner. No tension, no late swing, just a forward line on industrial action.
assessment: Nicolas built his 38 narrowly but effectively. João Pedro 11 and Tavernier 10 gave him 21, and nine of his eleven scored, which was more than enough.
Stefano's 28 is the week's floor. Saka 9 and Cherki 8 produced 17, which means nine starters delivered 11. The front three gave him nought, nought and nought.
There was no escape on either bench. This was not a selection error, it was simply a bad squad week.
The release rule then inverts the result entirely. Nicolas wins by ten and pays the higher fee, so in squad terms the gap narrows even as the table records a hiding.
Stefano Babiolakis v Nicolas Rubin.overall: Nicolas takes the points and pays the higher release fee, which is the rule working exactly as written and exactly as nobody wants.

ledger_note: The rule did more damage to the winners than the losers in three of five fixtures. The largest single score in the league, De Cuyper's 17, was invisible to it entirely because Matthew Lees left him out.
moves_note: No waiver or free agent activity recorded. Every figure on this page is a pure draft outcome, which will stop being true the moment anyone touches the wire.
table_note: The five winners are separated only by points scored, so the order at the top is a beauty contest rather than a gap. The genuine anomaly is Roscoe Hill in sixth on zero points with 44 for, a higher total than four of the five managers above him.

awards.title: Biggest winner
awards.body: Top score of the week at 47, the tightest win of the week, and the broadest base in the league: four players on 37 between them and only Ballard blanking.

awards.title: Unluckiest manager
awards.body: Scored 44, a total that would have beaten the other eight managers in the league, and lost by three to the one it would not. Then handed over Palmer as a leaving present.

awards.title: Worst benching
awards.body: De Cuyper on 17 left out in a four-point defeat, with 19 unused points in total. Mark Stone wasted more in aggregate, but Mark won his fixture, so the consequence lands here.

awards.title: Most painful release
awards.body: Gakpo on 12, which is 35.3 per cent of his entire score, the highest proportional cost in the league. He lost the fixture by three as well.

awards.title: Best strategic move
awards.body: Won the fixture and gave back an eleven-point return nobody expects twice, while keeping the defensive block that actually built his 37.

awards.title: Most absurd
awards.body: Three forwards fielded, nought from all three, lost by ten, and punished less severely by the release rule than the man who beat him.

overall: A week in which the release rule did more damage to the winners than the losers in three of five fixtures. Piers Rennie won with a side whose best player managed six. Michael Lavarack won with Haaland on two.
